title: Sufficient Color Contrast
statement: For sampled normal-sized text with a measurable background, require a minimum foreground/background contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1. Large text, non-text controls, and unsampled backgrounds require separate evidence; this result is not a complete accessibility certification.
failureCondition: The minimum observed contrast ratio for applicable normal-sized text is below 4.5 to 1, or the required normal-text sample is unavailable.
counterexample: Light grey text (#999) on a white background (#FFF) yields a contrast ratio of approximately 2.85:1, failing the minimum requirement.
exceptionPolicy: Decorative text that conveys no information and disabled controls are exempt per WCAG 1.4.3.

provenance.rationale: Reconcile contrast advice with the normal-text measurement floor; broader accessibility needs separate evidence.

title: Minimum Interactive Target Size
statement: All interactive elements must have a minimum touch and click target area to prevent accidental activation and support motor-impaired users.
failureCondition: An interactive element renders with a clickable area smaller than 44x44 CSS pixels on any supported viewport.
counterexample: A 24x24 pixel icon button with no padding provides an insufficient target area, causing frequent mis-taps on mobile devices.
exceptionPolicy: Inline text links within a paragraph are exempt when the paragraph itself provides sufficient surrounding spacing.

provenance.rationale: Use the skill's 44-pixel touch recommendation as a conservative project target, not a universal statutory minimum.

title: Keyboard Navigation Coverage
statement: Every interactive element must be reachable and operable using only keyboard input, with a visible focus indicator, to support users who cannot use a pointer device.
failureCondition: An interactive element cannot receive focus via Tab key, or an action cannot be triggered via Enter or Space key, or the focus indicator is invisible.
counterexample: A div with an onClick handler but no tabIndex, role, or keyDown handler is invisible to keyboard users and fails this rule.

provenance.rationale: Require task-specific keyboard observation; focusability alone cannot prove that controls operate.

title: Screen Reader State Announcements
statement: Dynamic content changes that affect the user's current context must be announced to assistive technology through ARIA live regions or equivalent mechanisms.
failureCondition: A visible state change occurs (e.g., loading completion, error message, content update) without a corresponding ARIA live region announcement or focus management.
counterexample: A form submission that silently replaces the page content without announcing the result leaves a screen reader user unaware that anything happened.

provenance.rationale: Require observation of state announcements; DOM markers alone cannot establish assistive-technology behavior.

title: Motion Reduction Respect
statement: Interfaces that use motion or animation must provide a reduced-motion alternative that preserves all information and functionality without relying on movement.
failureCondition: An animation conveys information or triggers a workflow step, and no static alternative exists when prefers-reduced-motion is active.
counterexample: A progress indicator that only shows completion through an animated bar and disappears when reduced motion is enabled, leaving users without progress feedback.
exceptionPolicy: Essential motion requires a documented justification and an observed equivalent path; duration alone does not establish an exemption.

provenance.rationale: Retain motion-alternative review as an explicit requirement without declaring completion from an emulation flag.

title: Content Reflow Without Loss
statement: When the viewport narrows, content must reflow without losing information or functionality. Preserve access to genuinely two-dimensional content through a documented, usable scrolling region.
failureCondition: At 320 CSS pixels viewport width, content overflows horizontally, information is clipped without a scroll affordance, or interactive elements become unreachable.
counterexample: A data table that renders with fixed column widths and clips cell content on narrow viewports, hiding data without any indication.
exceptionPolicy: Data tables may use horizontal scrolling if the scroll affordance is clearly visible and all content remains accessible.

provenance.rationale: Bind narrow-layout evaluation to measured supported width and explicit overflow/reachability evidence.

title: Viewport Adaptation Testing
statement: Interfaces must be verified at multiple viewport breakpoints to confirm layout integrity, interaction patterns, and content hierarchy are preserved across screen sizes.
failureCondition: The interface was verified at fewer than three distinct viewport widths, or no evidence exists for mobile, tablet, and desktop breakpoints.
counterexample: Testing only at a 1920px desktop width and shipping without checking 375px or 768px viewports.
exceptionPolicy: Platform-specific native apps that target a single form factor may reduce the breakpoint requirement.

provenance.rationale: Retain a minimum multiple-width verification policy; viewport count does not establish all responsive behavior.

title: Explicit State Machine Definition
statement: Interactive workflows must define their state transitions explicitly before implementation to ensure all states, including error and recovery states, are accounted for.
failureCondition: States are discovered during implementation rather than designed, resulting in missing error handling, impossible state combinations, or unhandled edge cases.
counterexample: A multi-step checkout form where the 'payment failed but items reserved' state was never designed, causing users to lose their cart when payment retries.
exceptionPolicy: Purely static content pages without user interaction state are exempt.

provenance.rationale: Translate state-design guidance into a reviewable transition-definition obligation with chronology evidence.

title: Error Recovery Preservation
statement: When an operation fails, the interface must preserve the user's in-progress work and provide a clear recovery path that does not require re-entering lost data.
failureCondition: A failed operation (network error, validation error, timeout) causes loss of user input, forces a page reload, or returns to a blank initial state.
counterexample: A form submission that fails due to a network timeout and clears all fields, forcing the user to re-enter everything from scratch.

provenance.rationale: Require a failure-and-recovery journey that observes preserved user data rather than a state-name declaration.

title: Semantic Token Usage Over Raw Values
statement: Visual properties must reference semantic design tokens rather than raw color codes, pixel values, or magic numbers, enabling centralized theming and contrast reasoning.
failureCondition: Component styles contain hardcoded color hex codes, raw pixel values for spacing, or literal font sizes instead of referencing semantic tokens.
counterexample: Using color: #3B82F6 directly in a component instead of referencing var(--color-primary) or a semantic token, making theme changes impossible without find-and-replace.
exceptionPolicy: One-off values in SVG paths and third-party embed overrides may use raw values with a documented exception.

provenance.rationale: Translate semantic-token guidance into a source-review requirement with documented exceptions.

title: Single Emphasis Budget Per Surface
statement: Each visual surface must establish a clear emphasis hierarchy with a limited budget of highlighted elements, so users can identify the primary action or information at a glance.
failureCondition: More than three elements compete for primary visual emphasis on a single surface, or no element is visually distinguishable as the primary focal point.
counterexample: A dashboard where every card has a bold colored header, large icon, and animated badge, making all cards equally loud and preventing users from finding the most important metric.
exceptionPolicy: Data-dense operational dashboards may increase the budget with documented justification.

provenance.rationale: Retain the existing one-to-three emphasis budget as a review heuristic, not an externally mandated threshold.

title: Heading Structure Integrity
statement: Pages must use a single h1 element and maintain a logical heading hierarchy (h1 > h2 > h3) without skipping levels, to support both visual scanning and assistive technology navigation.
failureCondition: A page has zero or multiple h1 elements, or heading levels are skipped (e.g., h1 followed directly by h3).
counterexample: A page with three h1 elements for branding, navigation title, and content title, followed by an h4 for a subsection, breaking both semantic structure and screen reader navigation.

provenance.rationale: Retain a single-primary-heading project convention, checked on rendered pages rather than claimed as universal law.

title: Testable Acceptance Criteria
statement: Every user-facing requirement must include a measurable or observable acceptance criterion that can determine whether the implementation satisfies the requirement.
failureCondition: A requirement is written as a vague feature description (e.g., 'make it user-friendly') with no measurable outcome that can confirm success or failure.
counterexample: A requirement stating 'the dashboard should be fast' without specifying a target load time, interaction latency, or measurement methodology.
exceptionPolicy: Exploratory prototypes may defer formal acceptance criteria to the next iteration.

provenance.rationale: Require acceptance criteria tied to observable outcomes and explicit validation methods.

title: Evidence Tier Accompanies Claims
statement: Every design quality claim must be accompanied by its evidence tier classification so downstream consumers can distinguish measured results from heuristic opinions.
failureCondition: A quality claim is presented without disclosing whether it is based on automated measurement, manual observation, heuristic review, or expert opinion.
counterexample: An AI-generated accessibility audit presented as equivalent to a human expert review without disclosing the evidence tier or methodology limitations.

provenance.rationale: Carry evidence classes with claims so automated and owner/user observations cannot be conflated.

title: Severity Derived From Measured Impact
statement: Finding severity must be based on measured or observed user impact rather than subjective tone, ensuring that the most impactful issues are prioritized for resolution.
failureCondition: Severity is assigned based on personal preference, writing style, or political priority rather than user impact data or task failure rates.
counterexample: A cosmetic alignment issue rated as 'critical' because the reporter used strong language, while a task-blocking error was rated 'low' because it was reported matter-of-factly.
exceptionPolicy: Security vulnerabilities may use a separate severity framework independent of UX impact.

provenance.rationale: Require impact-based severity reasoning, retaining uncertainty where user-impact evidence is unavailable.

title: Component Boundary Data Ownership
statement: Each component must own its data boundaries, with state lifted only through explicit interfaces, to prevent cross-component coupling and cascading breakage.
failureCondition: A component directly reads or mutates another component's internal state, or global state changes in one component cause unexpected behavior in unrelated components.
counterexample: A dashboard widget that directly accesses and modifies the state of a navigation component, causing the sidebar to collapse when the widget refreshes data.
exceptionPolicy: Shared application-level state managers (Redux, Zustand) are acceptable when access patterns are documented.

provenance.rationale: Translate explicit component ownership guidance into a review of state and dependency boundaries.

title: Stage Gate Before Stage Start
statement: Multi-stage workflows must verify that preceding stage outputs satisfy the next stage's input requirements before allowing progression, preventing downstream failures from incomplete inputs.
failureCondition: A workflow stage accepts inputs from a previous stage without validation, resulting in errors, data corruption, or silent failures that surface only at a later stage.
counterexample: A design-to-code handoff that proceeds without verifying that all required design tokens are defined, causing the code generation stage to produce invalid output.
exceptionPolicy: Purely informational preview stages may skip gate validation.

provenance.rationale: Require stage entry prerequisites to be validated; successful later output does not prove the earlier gate existed.

title: Handoff Manifest Completeness
statement: Design-to-development handoffs must include a structured manifest listing all deliverables, their completion status, known limitations, and unfinished items, so the receiving team can make an informed acceptance decision.
failureCondition: A handoff consists of a folder of files without a manifest, leaving the receiving team unable to determine what is complete, what is missing, and what is intentionally deferred.
counterexample: Handing off a Figma file and a ZIP of assets with no indication of which screens are final, which are placeholder, and which edge cases remain undesigned.
exceptionPolicy: Internal team iterations with continuous collaboration may use lightweight handoff notes instead of formal manifests.

provenance.rationale: Require handoff manifests to enumerate deliverables and unresolved gaps before acceptance.
